Based on the provided documents, the Apollo 13 accident in oxygen tank no. 2 began at 55:54:53.550 g.e.t. with the loss of telemetry data.

On Apollo 11, the circulation of the cabin atmosphere through lithium hydroxide filters continued during the return to Earth to remove trace particulate material after cleaning. 

On Apollo 13, because the lunar module lithium hydroxide cartridges would become ineffective due to saturation, and Command Module (CM) canisters were shaped differently, Manned Spacecraft Center engineers devised a procedure for the crew to build a modified container using onboard materials. This allowed the use of CM LiOH canisters in the LM cabin atmosphere cleaning system, successfully maintaining carbon dioxide partial pressure below 2 mm Hg for the remainder of the return trip.
ground_truth: In Apollo 11, lithium hydroxide filters in the environmental control system were used during cabin cleanup to capture abrasive airborne lunar dust after surface EVAs. In Apollo 13, lithium hydroxide canisters were critical consumables used to scrub carbon dioxide from the atmosphere; after the accident, ground controllers devised a procedure using spacesuit hoses, cue cards, and plastic bags to adapt square Command Module LiOH canisters for use in the Lunar Module's cylindrical system.
